title: How old are you?
title_target: Сколько вам лет? — Skolko vam let?
goal: Count to a hundred, give phone numbers and ages — and discover that in Russian your age isn't something you have but something given to you.
bekal: give and ask for a phone number
say your age with Мне … лет
choose год / года / лет to match the number
use сколько to ask about anything

dialogs.title: Диалог — Filling in a library card form
dialogs.intro: Ani is signing up at the campus library. The librarian, Нина, fills in the form as she asks questions. Notice that Ani never says "I am twenty-one" — in Russian her age is given to her.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.literal: eight — nine-hundred — twelve, three-hundred — forty — five, sixty — seven.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Eight… nine… one… two… Is that easier?
lines.literal: eight… nine… one… two… so — easier?

lines.speaker: Нина:
lines.id: Much easier. How many books do you want to take?
lines.literal: much-more. how-many — books — you — want — to-take?

lines.speaker: Нина:
lines.id: You can take five. Here's your card.
lines.literal: allowed — five — books (another form), here-is — your — card.

notes: **In Russian your age is given to you, not owned by you.** ⚠️ *Мне двадцать один год* is literally "to me twenty-one year". "I" becomes **мне** — the dative form — and there is no verb at all. English speakers almost always try *Я двадцать один год* (copying "I am twenty-one"), which is wrong, or *У меня двадцать один год* (copying French or Italian "I have"), also wrong. Only **Мне … лет** is correct.

**Год / года / лет — the last digit decides.** This is your first meeting with a big rule that applies to every noun after a number. The grammar box below has the whole rule; learn it through three examples: 21 год, 22 года, 25 лет.

**Лет is a special form.** Logically it should be годов, but Russian uses лет — an old form of the word лето (summer). So "twenty-five years" is literally "twenty-five summers". A leftover from the days when people counted their age in summers lived through.

**Phone numbers in Russia are read in groups, not digit by digit.** The standard pattern is 8-XXX-XXX-XX-XX, and people read it as numbers: *восемь, девятьсот двенадцать, триста сорок пять…*. ⚠️ If you're not fluent yet, reading it digit by digit is perfectly understandable — and often preferred by someone who is writing it down.

**Сколько is always followed by the genitive plural.** *Сколько книг?* (how many books), *Сколько денег?* (how much money), *Сколько лет?* (how many years). You don't need to master the genitive plural now; just notice that the word after сколько sounds clipped: книга → книг, рубль → рублей.

**Можно means "it's allowed" and stands on its own, without a subject.** *Можно?* by itself means "may I?". *Можно пять книг* — you can take five books. The opposite is **нельзя** (not allowed). These two words will save you again and again.
**Ещё раз** (*yi-SHCHO ras*) — "once more". Another lifesaver, a partner to *Повторите, пожалуйста* from Unit 1.

grammars.title: Numbers 0–100
body: The numbers 11–19 all end in **-надцать** ("on top of ten") — like English -teen. The tens 50, 60, 70, 80 end in **-десят** ("ten") — like English -ty.
after: ⚠️ Two numbers break the pattern and must be learned separately: **сорок** (40, not четыредесят) and **девяносто** (90, not девятьдесят). Both are leftovers from an old Russian counting system.
Compound numbers are simply strung together: 21 = двадцать один, 47 = сорок семь, 100 = сто. No "and", no hyphen.

grammars.title: The number decides the form of the noun ⚠️
body: This rule applies to **every** noun after a number, not just "year". What counts is the **last digit**, not the whole number.
after: ⚠️ The numbers 11, 12, 13 and 14 always use the third row even though they end in 1–4: **11 лет**, **12 лет**, **13 лет**, **14 лет**. Don't forget this exception — it happens to cover the school-age years people mention most.
Full examples: *Мне 1 год. Мне 22 года. Мне 25 лет. Мне 31 год. Мне 44 года. Мне 12 лет.*
If you really forget the form mid-conversation, just say the number: *Мне двадцать пять.* Russians often do this themselves, and there's nothing wrong with it.

blocks.title: Numbers in everyday life
items: **House and floor numbers** are read as ordinary numbers: *дом 5, квартира 12, этаж 3*.
**Prices** use рубль: *сто рублей* (100 rubles), *двести пятьдесят рублей* (250 rubles). Unit 8 covers this fully.
**Children's ages** most often use лет, since 5–20 covers almost every school age: *Ему 7 лет.* — He's 7.
⚠️ **Ноль** and **нуль** are both correct for "zero", but in phone numbers Russians usually say **ноль**. Same for temperatures: *ноль градусов*.
